appraisal_events.evidence: « l'avenir qu'il avait dans l'armée, sa situation mondaine, sa famille [...] ne comptait en rien auprès des moindres choses qui concernaient sa maîtresse » ; « Cela seul avait pour lui du prestige, infiniment plus de prestige que les Guermantes et tous les rois de la terre » ; « il envisageait la perspective d'un brillant mariage, seulement pour pouvoir continuer à l'entretenir » ; « il sentait que cet amour qu'elle avait pour lui n'empêchait pas qu'elle ne restât avec lui qu'à cause de son argent ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, speaking with flat expository authority rather than irony, shows Saint-Loup's rank, army career and Guermantes name emptied of all value beside his mistress, and shows him holding her only by money and by the calculated withholding of marriage. The tenderness of his talk qualifies the tone but the dominant local movement is the exposure of a nobleman reduced to purchased and suspicious dependence.

appraisal_events.evidence: « elle a surtout un jugement merveilleux [...] elle dit des choses qu'on peut approfondir indéfiniment, elle a vraiment quelque chose de pythique » ; « elle n'est pas extraordinaire comme figure, tu sais (je vis bien qu'il pensait tout le contraire et ne disait cela que pour que mon admiration fût plus grande) ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup builds his mistress up before the narrator as an oracular intelligence and prices her beyond any sum, which locally elevates her. The narrator immediately catches the rhetorical staging of the praise, so the elevation is reported as Saint-Loup's inflation rather than confirmed by the narration.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup is shown as wholly at his mistress's mercy — capable of suffering, of happiness, perhaps of killing through her — while suspecting she stays for his money; all local leverage lies with her.

His aristocratic assets are locally devalued by his own reckoning and instrumentalized: the Guermantes name counts for nothing and a brilliant marriage is contemplated merely as a way of financing his mistress.
She holds complete emotional and practical leverage over Saint-Loup: she alone has prestige for him, she is priceless in his estimation, and he must keep her by expectation of tomorrow's gifts.

ambiguities: The mistress is never named in the passage (« son amie », « sa maîtresse »); identifying her as Rachel depends on wider context rather than on anything in these paragraphs, so the target of E2 is resolved by inference.

The passage's stance toward Saint-Loup is genuinely double: it opens by praising the tenderness of his talk and the absoluteness of his devotion, then dismantles that devotion as bought and mistrustful. The diminishment reading is taken as dominant because the explanatory weight of the passage falls on money, calculation and the fear of being left.
